cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: Which four real contracts does Roman law recognise?
cards.back:
MUTUUM, DEPOSITUM, COMMODATUM and PIGNUS — each arises only when a thing is actually handed over.
• MUTUUM = interest-free loan for consumption.
• DEPOSITUM = gratuitous safekeeping (deposit).
• COMMODATUM = gratuitous loan for use; PIGNUS = real contract of pledge.
• PRECARIUM is similar, but the jurists treated it as a factual arrangement, not a contract.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: What two elements make up every real contract?
cards.back:
CONVENTIO (agreement) plus DATIO (actual handover); the obligation arises only once the thing has been delivered.
• CONVENTIO fixes the purpose of the transfer — and thus which real contract it is.
• It can also fix further terms, e.g. the duration.
• CONVENTIO alone is not enough: no DATIO, no real contract.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: Property effect of the DATIO: in which real contracts does the recipient become owner, and in which only detentor?
cards.back:
Owner (and proprietary possessor) in MUTUUM and DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE; mere detentor (natural possession) in all other real contracts.
• MUTUUM: the borrower must be able to spend the money — so he needs ownership.
• DEPOSITUM, COMMODATUM, PIGNUS: the recipient only holds the thing for the giver.
• Hence there the very same thing must come back.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: Property link: possessor vs detentor — what is the difference, and who is which in the real contracts?
cards.back:
A possessor holds the thing for himself (ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI); a detentor holds it for someone else (NATURALIS POSSESSIO).
• MUTUUM borrower: owner and proprietary possessor.
• Depositary and commodatary: detentors — they hold for the giver.
• Pledgee, precarist, SEQUESTER: natural possessors too, yet protected by possessory interdicts.
• Possession is a fact (control plus intent); ownership is the right to the thing.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: Are Roman real contracts gratuitous?
cards.back:
In principle yes; the one exception is DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, where the recipient may use the money but owes interest.
• Paid safekeeping or paid use = LOCATIO CONDUCTIO, not a real contract.
• MUTUUM itself carries no interest; interest needs another basis, e.g. a STIPULATIO.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: What is a MUTUUM?
cards.back:
Interest-free loan for consumption: the lender transfers ownership of money or other fungibles; the borrower returns an equal quantity of the same kind.
• Formula: TANTUNDEM EIUSDEM GENERIS REDDERE — return as much of the same kind.
• Not the same coins or grain come back, only equivalents.
• Being gratuitous, it served mostly loans between friends.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: What are fungible goods, and why does MUTUUM require them?
cards.back:
Things normally dealt in by quantity, number or weight, where the identity of each piece does not matter — e.g. money, grain, olives.
• The borrower consumes the goods and returns other pieces of the same kind.
• That only works if the pieces are interchangeable.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: What are the five requirements of a MUTUUM?
cards.back:
Loan CONVENTIO, actual DATIO, fungible assets, lender's ownership or power of disposal, and the borrower's acquisition of ownership.
• Lender not owner → initially no MUTUUM (Case 6: thief lends stolen money).
• DATIO and CONVENTIO differ in amount → MUTUUM only for the smaller sum (Case 1).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: Property link: how does ownership pass to the borrower in a MUTUUM?
cards.back:
By TRADITIO: transferor's ownership or authority, handover of possession, and a IUSTA CAUSA — the loan itself is a recognised IUSTA CAUSA TRADITIONIS.
• NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET: a non-owner cannot pass ownership.
• So a lender who is not owner cannot make a full MUTUUM (Case 6).
• Repayment works the same way: the returned coins become the lender's again.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: Who bears the risk of accidental loss in a MUTUUM?
cards.back:
CASUM SENTIT DOMINUS: the lender until the DATIO, the borrower afterwards — he must repay regardless of fault.
• As new owner the borrower carries damage, loss or destruction.
• Matches the economic purpose: the assets enter the borrower's estate.
• Special rule for the CONTRACTUS MOHATRAE: risk follows interest (Case 3).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: FENUS NAUTICUM vs ordinary MUTUUM — how is the risk split?
cards.back:
In the maritime loan the lender shares the venture's risk: ship lost → no repayment; ship arrives → principal plus interest.
• Greek origin; financed sea trade.
• Resembles a partnership or insurance.
• Ordinary MUTUUM: the borrower repays whatever happens.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: Which action does the lender have under a MUTUUM, and what is it called for money and for produce?
cards.back:
The CONDICTIO — a IUDICIUM STRICTI IURIS for a CERTA RES (thing or quantity) or a CERTA PECUNIA (sum).
• Money loans: ACTIO CERTAE CREDITAE PECUNIAE.
• Loaned produce: CONDICTIO TRITICARIA (TRITICUM = wheat).
• Claims the equivalent in kind, quantity and quality — not the very items.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: What can the lender recover by the loan condiction, and why is it so efficient for him?
cards.back:
Only TANTUNDEM EIUSDEM GENERIS, no interest; he need only allege and prove the delivery.
• Other aspects of the relationship are in principle irrelevant in court.
• Interest needs another basis, e.g. a STIPULATIO — hence big commercial loans by stipulation.
• Lender in blatant bad faith → borrower raises the EXCEPTIO DOLI.
• Harm in performing (pest-infested grain) → ACTIO DE DOLO or EXCEPTIO DOLI.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: Property link: why does the lender sue by CONDICTIO and not by REI VINDICATIO?
cards.back:
After the DATIO the borrower owns the coins; REI VINDICATIO is the owner's action in rem, so the lender has only a personal claim.
• REI VINDICATIO: owner against any possessor, for the thing itself, only while it exists.
• CONDICTIO: action in personam for an equivalent sum or quantity.
• Case 6: owner E may vindicate while the coins exist; once spent, only condictions remain.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: Ulpian (Proculus) D 12.1.11.1 (Case 1): A hands B 10 coins, but they agree B owes 9. What is the loan debt?
cards.back:
9 — the DATIO counts as MUTUUM only up to the agreed amount.
• The CONVENTIO limits the DATIO.
• 10th coin: B may keep it if A gave it on purpose (possibly a gift).
• If B repays it by mistake → CONDICTIO INDEBITI.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: General remarks and MUTUUM
cards.front: Ulpian (Proculus) D 12.1.11.1 (Case 1): A hands B 10 coins, but they agree B owes 11. What is the loan debt?
cards.back:
10 — a MUTUUM cannot exceed what was actually delivered; there is no action for the 11th coin.
• The DATIO limits the CONVENTIO.
• To owe 11, a STIPULATIO is needed — for the extra coin or for all eleven.
• Lesson: CONVENTIO and DATIO together set the debt; the smaller amount wins.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: Which three special forms of loan also gave the lender the CONDICTIO by the end of the classical period?
cards.back:
Loan by assignment/delegation, loan by agreement, and the CONTRACTUS MOHATRAE.
• Delegation: a third party pays the borrower from the third party's own funds.
• Agreement: B already owes L money and may keep it for a time as a loan.
• MOHATRA: L gives goods to sell; B keeps the proceeds as the loan.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: Loan by assignment/delegation: how does it work, and how does it differ from the basic MUTUUM?
cards.back:
L instructs his debtor TP to pay B; TP's payment discharges TP's debt to L and creates a MUTUUM between L and B.
• As if L had collected from TP and lent the money on to B.
• Needs a loan CONVENTIO between L and B plus TP's actual payment.
• Real DATIO and transfer of ownership — but the assets were never the lender's.
• Oldest special form: accepted already classically, for practical purposes.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: Julian vs Ulpian: do the loan by agreement and the CONTRACTUS MOHATRAE create a MUTUUM?
cards.back:
High-classical Julian: no CONDICTIO for either; late-classical Ulpian: both are MUTUUM.
• Julian: no DATIO — mere agreement (NUDA PACTIONE) cannot create a MUTUUM (Case 4).
• Julian's fallback in Case 4: the ACTIO MANDATI.
• Ulpian: agreement suffices (Case 2); MOHATRA = MUTUUM once the goods are sold (Case 3).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: Ulpian D 12.1.15 (Case 2): appointee B must pay mandate money to principal A; they agree B may keep it for his business. MUTUUM?
cards.back:
Yes — A has the CONDICTIO; an agreement between creditor and debtor suffices, no physical DATIO needed.
• Analogy to the loan by delegation: if two persons can play the roles, one can play both.
• Shortcut: strictly B would hand the money to A, and A straight back as a loan.
• Ulpian skips the back-and-forth and treats both transfers as done.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: Ulpian (Nerva) D 12.1.11 pr (Case 3): A gives B a bowl to sell, B to keep the proceeds as a loan. When is there a MUTUUM, and who bears accidental loss before the sale?
cards.back:
MUTUUM once B sells (buyer's payment = DATIO); risk before the sale depends on whose interest and initiative drove the deal.
• Sale mainly in A's interest (B just a sales agent) → A bears the loss.
• A sold only to lend B the proceeds → B bears the risk.
• A then claims the value, presumably by ACTIO PRAESCRIPTIS VERBIS (innominate contract; cf Case 210).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: Africanus (Julian) D 17.1.34 pr (Case 4): procurator P has collected L's money and by letter borrows it from L at 6 % interest. MUTUUM?
cards.back:
No — no DATIO, and NUDA PACTIONE cannot create a MUTUUM; L sues by ACTIO MANDATI for principal and interest.
• Deferring the handover = consensual modification of the original mandate.
• As BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM it covers the 6 % interest; downside: every defence can be raised.
• Loan serves only P's interest → P bears even accidental loss (utility principle).
• Julian adds: the CONTRACTUS MOHATRAE is likewise no MUTUUM.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: Case 4: why is the procurator's arrangement neither TRADITIO BREVI MANU nor a loan on order?
cards.back:
P already owned and possessed the collected money, so no BREVI MANU was possible; the loan agreement came only after he received it.
• BREVI MANU needs a detentor who becomes possessor — like depositary Y with depositor R.
• Loan on order needs a prior CONVENTIO under which the recipient takes from the third party.
• The idea of a procurator acquiring directly for his principal plays no part.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: Property link: what is TRADITIO BREVI MANU, and how does it turn a deposit into a MUTUUM?
cards.back:
A detentor becomes possessor by mere agreement — no return and redelivery; with a loan as CAUSA he thereby also becomes owner.
• The depositary holds for the depositor (detentor); CORPUS already exists.
• Parties agree on a loan: he now holds for himself (POSSESSOR).
• Change of CONVENTIO plus BREVI MANU = the loan's DATIO.
• Ownership passes only if the depositor has authority to dispose.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: Ulpian D 12.1.13 pr (Case 6): thief G lends money stolen from E to N, who takes it in good faith and spends it. Claims?
cards.back:
Initially no MUTUUM (G is no owner); once N mixes or spends the coins, a CONDICTIO lies against N — presumably in G's hands.
• Before spending: E is still owner → REI VINDICATIO against N.
• At that stage G has no claim: no MUTUUM, no enrichment condiction.
• Spending gives N the economic value — the loan convalesces.
• E keeps ACTIO FURTI and CONDICTIO FURTIVA against thief G.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: Case 6: why does Ulpian let the loan between thief and borrower convalesce?
cards.back:
Most likely to protect the victim E — not the thief or N.
• E can make the thief assign him the condiction against (presumably solvent) N.
• Better than relying only on CONDICTIO FURTIVA or ACTIO FURTI against a possibly insolvent thief.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: Property link: what is NUMMOS CONSUMERE, and what does it do to the former owner's rights?
cards.back:
Mixing coins indistinguishably with one's own, or spending them in good faith, gives original ownership; the former owner loses his REI VINDICATIO.
• Reason: flexible cash management; coins are hard to trace.
• Former owner keeps only personal claims: CONDICTIO, or CONDICTIO FURTIVA against a thief.
• Hence borrower N in Case 6 becomes owner after all.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: What is the SENATUS CONSULTUM MACEDONIANUM, and why was it passed?
cards.back:
A senatorial decree (dated 69–79 AD) to stop loans to sons and daughters under PATRIA POTESTAS.
• Children in power owned nothing; aim: shield them from debt and creditor pressure.
• Also from dubious ways of raising money.
• Trigger: son Macedo, hounded by creditors, murdered his PATER FAMILIAS (Ulpian D 14.6.1 pr).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: How does the praetor protect a borrowing child in power under the SC MACEDONIANUM?
cards.back:
Either he himself denies the lender the CONDICTIO, or he inserts an EXCEPTIO SENATUS CONSULTI MACEDONIANI and leaves the decision to the IUDEX.
• The EXCEPTIO lets the child defeat the repayment claim.
• Praetor sets the programme (ACTIO, EXCEPTIO); the IUDEX executes it.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: How far does the SC MACEDONIANUM reach — and when does it not protect?
cards.back:
Covers sureties, survives the borrower becoming SUI IURIS, catches evasive deals — but not a son who fraudulently posed as SUI IURIS.
• A surety may also raise the EXCEPTIO SC MACEDONIANI.
• Evasion: goods handed over to be sold, proceeds kept as loan (Ulpian D 14.6.7.3, Case 8).
• Fraud by posing as SUI IURIS: Pertinax C 4.28.1 (Case 9a).
• Approval of the loan by the PATER FAMILIAS excludes the SC.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: What is the legal quality of a loan caught by the SC MACEDONIANUM?
cards.back:
A natural obligation: the repayment claim exists but is unenforceable because of the EXCEPTIO.
• If repaid anyway, the lender may keep the money.
• The child cannot reclaim it as payment of a non-existent debt.
• The lender's ACTIO ADIECTICIAE QUALITATIS against the PATER FAMILIAS is not barred.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: Julian D 14.6.14 (Case 7): A holds power over son B and grandson C; C borrows from D on B's order. Does B's approval exclude the SC MACEDONIANUM?
cards.back:
No — only approval by the holder of power (A) excludes the SC; B is C's father, but not his PATER FAMILIAS.
• Rule: PATER FAMILIAS approves the loan → the SC does not apply.
• B is himself in A's power.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Special loans, unauthorised holder, SC MACEDONIANUM
cards.front: Paulus D 14.6.17 (Case 10): son B borrows from X to give his sister C a dowry. Can X recover?
cards.back:
Not from B (SC MACEDONIANUM), but from father A by the ACTIO DE IN REM VERSO.
• Providing the dowry was A's duty; paying it from X's loan enriched A (VERSIO).
• Proof: A may claim the DOS back if C dies during the marriage.
• So B's provision counts as fulfilment of A's duty.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: DEPOSITUM and the principle of utility
cards.front: What is a DEPOSITUM?
cards.back:
A thing is handed to someone who agrees to keep it safe gratuitously; in principle the very same items must be returned.
• Fungibles and non-fungibles can be deposited.
• Unlike MUTUUM, the depositor's ownership is generally irrelevant.
• Animals: custody includes feeding and care (cf § 957 ABGB).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: DEPOSITUM and the principle of utility
cards.front: DEPOSITUM, COMMODATUM, LOCATIO CONDUCTIO — how do they differ when a thing is handed over?
cards.back:
Gratuitous custody = DEPOSITUM; gratuitous use = COMMODATUM; custody or use for payment = LOCATIO CONDUCTIO.
• Paid deposit: LOCATIO CONDUCTIO (cf Ulpian D 16.3.1.8, Case 11).
• Paid use: LOCATIO CONDUCTIO REI (lease/rent).
• MUTUUM differs from all: ownership passes, only equivalents come back.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: DEPOSITUM and the principle of utility
cards.front: May the depositary use the deposited thing?
cards.back:
No — unauthorised use of the deposit is FURTUM.
• Gai Inst 3.196: ITAQUE SI QUIS RE QUAE APUD EUM DEPOSITA SIT UTATUR, FURTUM COMMITTIT.
• Agreed use of deposited money changes the deal (MUTUUM or DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: DEPOSITUM and the principle of utility
cards.front: Which actions arise from a DEPOSITUM, and why is it imperfectly bilateral?
cards.back:
Depositor: ACTIO DEPOSITI DIRECTA (esp. return); depositary: ACTIO DEPOSITI CONTRARIA for expenses and losses; both BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA.
• Return claim always arises; counterclaims only possibly → imperfectly bilateral.
• E.g. feed costs; own livestock infected by diseased deposited animals.
• Depositary may retain until satisfied — no EXCEPTIO DOLI needed (BONAE FIDEI).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: DEPOSITUM and the principle of utility
cards.front: What is the principle of utility, and in which two ways does it work?
cards.back:
Contractual liability follows the distribution of interests: the party with the greater economic interest bears more of the risk.
• (a) Each contract type has a typical distribution of interests → primary risk allocation.
• (b) Concrete case deviates from the type → risk allocated differently.
• MOHATRA: normally recipient bears loss; if (also) in lender's interest → only for fault.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: DEPOSITUM and the principle of utility
cards.front: For what is the depositary liable, and why so little?
cards.back:
For DOLUS and conduct close to it — CULPA LATA and breach of DILIGENTIA QUAM IN SUIS REBUS — because custody is a favour.
• He pursues no economic aim of his own.
• CULPA LATA: Nerva in D 16.3.32 (Case 12).
• DILIGENTIA QUAM IN SUIS REBUS: less care than for own property → liable (Celsus, Case 12).
• Subjective standard: its breach = CULPA IN CONCRETO (vs CULPA IN ABSTRACTO).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: DEPOSITUM and the principle of utility
cards.front: Which risks does the depositor bear in a DEPOSITUM?
cards.back:
Damage through the depositary's slight negligence (CULPA LEVIS) and by accident (CASUS).
• The depositor normally stays owner → CASUM SENTIT DOMINUS.
• Theft of the deposit by a third party: the depositary is not liable (cf Case 28).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: DEPOSITUM and the principle of utility
cards.front: When does the depositary's liability rise above DOLUS?
cards.back:
When his own interest rises: if he pressed his services on the depositor, he answers for DOLUS, CULPA and CUSTODIA.
• Depositor then bears only VIS MAIOR — shiftable by agreement too (Ulpian D 16.3.1.35, Case 14).
• Dolose use without consent → liable for resulting accident: CASUS MIXTUS (Ulpian D 16.3.1.25, Case 15).
• Cf § 965 ABGB.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: DEPOSITUM and the principle of utility
cards.front: Property link: what does CASUM SENTIT DOMINUS mean for the real contracts?
cards.back:
The owner bears accidental loss: whoever owns the thing carries its accidental damage or destruction.
• MUTUUM, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE: recipient becomes owner → bears the loss, must repay anyway.
• DEPOSITUM, COMMODATUM: the giver stays owner → he bears CASUS or VIS MAIOR.
• Contractual liability (CULPA, CUSTODIA) and the utility principle shift this.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Deposit of money, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, SEQUESTRE
cards.front: How can a deposit of money be turned into a MUTUUM?
cards.back:
The parties change their CONVENTIO to a loan; by TRADITIO BREVI MANU the depositary becomes possessor and owner — this is the loan's DATIO.
• Sealed bag of coins = ordinary deposit, legally like any non-fungible thing.
• Usually a needy depositary asks; the depositor is content with the same amount back.
• Consequences: borrower bears the risk; lender sues by CONDICTIO.
• IUSTA CAUSA = the loan; ownership passes only with depositor's authority to dispose.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Deposit of money, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, SEQUESTRE
cards.front: Ulpian (Nerva, Proculus, Marcellus) D 12.1.9.9 (Case 16): A deposits 10 coins with B, later lets B use them; then the coins are taken out. When does the loan arise?
cards.back:
Already with the agreed change of the CONVENTIO and the accompanying TRADITIO BREVI MANU — not only when B takes the money out.
• From then B bears the risk for the 10 coins.
• A sues by CONDICTIO.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Deposit of money, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, SEQUESTRE
cards.front: Ulpian D 12.1.10 (Case 17): A deposits money with B and at the same time allows him to use it if he wishes. When does a loan arise?
cards.back:
Only once B actually removes the money from where it is kept — until then it remains a regular DEPOSITUM.
• Main aim is safekeeping; B's future need is uncertain (auxiliary agreement).
• A's permission = standing offer; B accepts it by taking the money.
• The taking also works as TRADITIO BREVI MANU → MUTUUM (or DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Deposit of money, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, SEQUESTRE
cards.front: Case 16 vs Case 17: why does the loan arise at different moments?
cards.back:
Case 16: a later agreement changes the CONVENTIO itself → loan at once; Case 17: permission at deposit is an option → loan on taking.
• Case 16: TRADITIO BREVI MANU accompanies the new agreement.
• Case 17: A's standing offer is accepted by B's taking.
• Practical point: who bears the risk before the money is removed.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Deposit of money, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, SEQUESTRE
cards.front: What is a DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE?
cards.back:
Money deposited with permission for the recipient to use it, with interest depending on the terms — between MUTUUM and DEPOSITUM, enforced by ACTIO DEPOSITI.
• The label is modern.
• Like a savings account: safety plus interest; the bank uses the funds, guarantees nominal value.
• The only exception to the gratuitousness of real contracts.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Deposit of money, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, SEQUESTRE
cards.front: Why is the DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE enforced by the ACTIO DEPOSITI, and how is it recognised?
cards.back:
The giver has a depositor's interest in safety, and the BONAE FIDEI ACTIO DEPOSITI accommodates special terms.
• Indicator: money handed over loose (open deposit), not sealed (cf Papinian D 16.3.25.1, Case 20).
• Ownership passes; the recipient may use the money (cf Alfenus D 19.2.31, Case 172).
• He must repay regardless of fault, as with a loan.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Deposit of money, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, SEQUESTRE
cards.front: DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE vs MUTUUM — what is common, what differs?
cards.back:
Both pass ownership and risk to the recipient; they differ in action, purpose and interest.
• Action: ACTIO DEPOSITI (BONAE FIDEI) vs CONDICTIO (STRICTI IURIS).
• Purpose: giver's interest in safety vs borrower's need for money.
• Interest: available through BONA FIDES vs never through the condiction (needs STIPULATIO).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Deposit of money, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, SEQUESTRE
cards.front: Paulus D 16.3.29.1 (Case 18): A deposits money with B, who uses it with A's consent. Does B owe interest?
cards.back:
Yes — as in all BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA, B owes interest (Paulus evidently means the DEPOSITUM).
• Interest derived from BONA FIDES, cleanly separated from MUTUUM and CONDICTIO.
• Unclear whether interest for use or default interest is meant.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Deposit of money, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, SEQUESTRE
cards.front: Papinian D 16.3.24 (Case 20 a): Lucius Titius confirms by letter that Sempronius handed him 100 coins for safekeeping (COMMENDASTI). Action, and interest?
cards.back:
COMMENDARE = deposit → ACTIO DEPOSITI; in this BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM the judge may award interest for use or for delay.
• Money taken as a favour to the giver → no interest before default.
• An agreement on interest for use must be respected.
• Middle part probably interpolated; final third presumably genuine Papinian.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Deposit of money, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, SEQUESTRE
cards.front: Scaevola D 16.3.28 (Case 20 b): C confirms in writing receiving 25.000 sesterces from P and promises interest. Enforceable?
cards.back:
Yes — a valid agreement on interest for use, enforced by the ACTIO DEPOSITI (BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM).
• Irrelevant whether C made a profit with the money or merely consumed it.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Deposit of money, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, SEQUESTRE
cards.front: Paulus Coll. 10.7.9 (Case 19): money deposited and (possibly later) its use permitted — MUTUA MAGIS VIDETUR QUAM DEPOSITA. Meaning?
cards.back:
The deal is nearer to a loan than to a deposit, so the taker bears the risk (PERICULUM).
• Unclear: deposit turned into MUTUUM (BREVI MANU) or into DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE.
• Either way the taker must repay regardless of fault.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Deposit of money, DEPOSITUM IRREGULARE, SEQUESTRE
cards.front: What is a DEPOSITUM SEQUESTRE?
cards.back:
Two parties disputing ownership deposit the thing with a third person (SEQUESTER), who hands it to the winner of the lawsuit.
• The SEQUESTER's possession is protected by possessory interdicts.
• The winner sues the SEQUESTER by the ACTIO DEPOSITI SEQUESTRARIA.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: COMMODATUM
cards.front: What is a COMMODATUM?
cards.back:
A thing is handed over (DATIO) for the recipient to use free of charge; the very same thing must be returned.
• Hence only non-consumables can be lent for use.
• Lender's ownership is irrelevant (unlike MUTUUM).
• Gratuitous favour; paid use = LOCATIO CONDUCTIO REI (rent).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: COMMODATUM
cards.front: How far may the commodatary use the borrowed thing?
cards.back:
He may use it while preserving its substance, within limits set by the agreement or BONA FIDES; exceeding them is FURTUM.
• Gai Inst 3.196: turning it to a different use → FURTI OBLIGATUR.
• Consequence: liability even for VIS MAIOR following the excess use (Case 23).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: COMMODATUM
cards.front: Which actions arise from a COMMODATUM, and who bears which costs?
cards.back:
Lender: ACTIO COMMODATI DIRECTA (esp. return); borrower: ACTIO COMMODATI CONTRARIA; BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM, imperfectly bilateral.
• Borrower carries ordinary operating costs (e.g. fodder).
• He recovers extraordinary expenses and losses caused by the loan.
• E.g. necessary vet costs for an illness unrelated to the use.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: COMMODATUM
cards.front: For what is the commodatary liable, and which risk stays with the lender?
cards.back:
Borrower: DOLUS, CULPA and CUSTODIA — the loan benefits only him; lender: VIS MAIOR, as owner (CASUM SENTIT DOMINUS).
• Fairly strict liability, by the utility principle.
• Avertable VIS MAIOR: failing to save the thing = CULPA (cf Paul Sent 2.4.2, Case 26).
• CUSTODIA covers e.g. theft by a third party (Case 28).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: COMMODATUM
cards.front: Compare the liability standards of depositary, commodatary and pledgee.
cards.back:
Depositary: DOLUS (+ CULPA LATA, DILIGENTIA QUAM IN SUIS REBUS); commodatary and pledgee: DOLUS, CULPA and CUSTODIA.
• Reason (utility): deposit serves the depositor; commodate and pledge serve the recipient.
• Depositor bears CULPA LEVIS and CASUS; commodator bears VIS MAIOR.
• Interests deviating from the type shift liability up or down.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: COMMODATUM
cards.front: Gaius D 13.6.18 pr (Case 23): what are the three rules on the commodatary's liability?
cards.back:
(1) Fault yes, VIS MAIOR no; (2) VIS MAIOR too if he exceeded permitted use; (3) lender's own interest lowers liability.
• (2) Excess use = FURTUM, and a FUR answers for every harm.
• Silverware taken on a journey, lost to shipwreck or pirates → borrower liable.
• (3) Both interested (joint dinner for mutual friends) → only CULPA (Gaius).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: COMMODATUM
cards.front: Lender also interested in the loan: Gaius vs Ulpian on the commodatary's liability?
cards.back:
Gaius: both parties interested → liable for CULPA; Ulpian: only DOLUS where agreed or where the loan served solely the lender.
• Gaius' example: C does the cooking, D supplies the silverware.
• Ulpian's example: jewels lent to wife or fiancée to be adorned for him (Ulpian D 13.6.5.10, Case 25).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: COMMODATUM
cards.front: Ulpian D 13.6.5.14 (Case 24): E lends T silverware; to avoid carrying it home, E leaves it at T's house overnight, where it is destroyed. Who bears the loss?
cards.back:
Labeo: E, if he posted his own guard; otherwise T. Ulpian: ACTIO COMMODATI — T answers for CUSTODIA unless otherwise agreed.
• Laying the table = mandate; lending the silver = commodate.
• Seen as overnight deposit? It serves the depositary → he is still liable.
• Labeo speaks of PERICULUM (VIS MAIOR?) — fits the commodate rules poorly.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: COMMODATUM
cards.front: Ulpian D 13.6.12.1 (Case 29): lender L's slave S collects the borrowed item from borrower B and runs off with it. Is B liable?
cards.back:
Depends on intent: if B handed it over to end the loan, his duty ended; if S only came to remind him, B is liable.
• Transfer of control over the thing matters for risk in a commodate.
• Handing it to a mere messenger is not an intended end of the loan.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: COMMODATUM
cards.front: Julian D 13.6.19 (Case 27): is the commodatary liable for damage caused to the borrowed thing by a third party (DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM)?
cards.back:
Generally no — that is beyond the CURA AUT DILIGENTIA reasonably expected of a commodatary.
• Not all jurists read CUSTODIA so narrowly (Ulpian D 19.2.41).
• Marcellus dissents: liable if preventable or caused by his own guards.
• Cf Julian: borrower cannot sue for borrowed clothes torn by a third party (Ulpian D 9.2.11.9).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: COMMODATUM
cards.front: Modestinus Coll 10.2.6 (Case 28): a lent thing is stolen from the commodatary by a third person. Who has the ACTIO FURTI?
cards.back:
The commodatary — under CUSTODIA liability he carries the loss, so he sues the thief.
• The lender recovers his loss from the borrower.
• Borrower insolvent → the owner must keep the right to sue the thief himself.
• Depositary: no ACTIO FURTI — nor needs one, as not liable for third-party theft.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: COMMODATUM
cards.front: Julian D 47.2.60 (59) (Case 30): A lends a thing to B and later secretly takes it back. Has B the ACTIO FURTI?
cards.back:
As a rule no — A took his own property, and this releases B from the duty to return it.
• Exception: B could retain the thing for necessary expenses → B has the ACTIO FURTI against A.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: COMMODATUM
cards.front: Modestinus Coll 10.2.5 (Case 31): who bears the maintenance costs of entrusted animals or slaves — depositary or commodatary?
cards.back:
The depositary may claim them in the ACTIO DEPOSITI, even without a separate counterclaim; the commodatary may not — he uses the thing.
• Deposit obliges him to keep the thing, not to pay for its upkeep.
• Commodatary does recover necessary costs of illness of a lent slave or animal.
• Such costs concern the owner's interest more than the user's.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: PRECARIUM and PIGNUS
cards.front: What is a PRECARIUM?
cards.back:
A factual grant of the use of a thing that the grantor may revoke unilaterally at any time — usually made at the recipient's request.
• Hence loan by entreaty (cf Ulpian D 43.26.1 pr, Case 33).
• Parallels the COMMODATUM (Ulpian D 43.26.1.3), but treated as factual, not a legal contract.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: PRECARIUM and PIGNUS
cards.front: How is the PRECARIO ACCIPIENS protected — and how does the PRECARIO DANS get the thing back?
cards.back:
Possessory interdicts against third parties, but not against the grantor (EXCEPTIO VITIOSAE POSSESSIONIS); the grantor also has the INTERDICTUM DE PRECARIO.
• Towards the grantor the recipient is an INIUSTUS POSSESSOR.
• He must give the thing back if he holds it, and cannot reclaim it if not.
• INTERDICTUM DE PRECARIO: restitution can be demanded at any time.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: PRECARIUM and PIGNUS
cards.front: What is the real contract of pledge (PIGNUS), and may the pledgee use the pledge?
cards.back:
One party gives a thing to another, agreed as security for a debt; as a rule the pledgee may not use it.
• Unauthorised use = FURTUM.
• Exception: antichresis — use of the pledge serves to (partly) pay off the debt.
• Contract valid even if the giver lacks power of disposal.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: PRECARIUM and PIGNUS
cards.front: Property link: PIGNUS as a right in rem vs PIGNUS as a real contract — how does each arise?
cards.back:
The right in rem arises without handover (secured debt, power of disposal, CONVENTIO PIGNORIS); the contract requires DATIO.
• Right in rem: VINDICATIO PIGNORIS against any possessor; ends with the debt.
• Contract: personal claims between pledger and pledgee (ACTIO PIGNERATICIA IN PERSONAM).
• Giver lacks power of disposal: contract yes, right in rem no.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: PRECARIUM and PIGNUS
cards.front: ACTIO PIGNERATICIA IN PERSONAM DIRECTA vs CONTRARIA — who claims what?
cards.back:
DIRECTA: pledger claims return or surplus; CONTRARIA: pledgee claims expenses, damage and a substitute pledge; both BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA.
• DIRECTA: return (plus damages) once the right of pledge ends, e.g. debt paid.
• DIRECTA: surplus of the sale proceeds over the debt (SUPERFLUUM, HYPEROCHA).
• CONTRARIA: substitute pledge if no right in rem arose (no power of disposal).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: PRECARIUM and PIGNUS
cards.front: For what is the pledgee liable, and why?
cards.back:
For DOLUS, CULPA and CUSTODIA — a possessory pledge serves only the pledgee's interest (principle of utility).
• The pledger gets no direct economic benefit from handing over.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Exercises (application)
cards.front: Ex 1: Aser informally agrees to lend his slave to Mirjam for the harvest, forgets and sends him elsewhere; hail destroys half her crop. Action under a COMMODATUM?
cards.back:
No — a COMMODATUM arises only with the DATIO; the mere CONVENTIO does not bind.
• Real contract = CONVENTIO + DATIO.
• The slave was never handed over → no ACTIO COMMODATI.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Exercises (application)
cards.front: Ex 3: Cato gives Drusus 2.000, repayable after a year; out of gratitude Drusus declares he will repay 2.200. Action and amount?
cards.back:
CONDICTIO (ACTIO CERTAE CREDITAE PECUNIAE) for 2.000 — the MUTUUM cannot exceed the DATIO.
• Parallel: Case 1 (10 delivered, 11 agreed → 10).
• The extra 200 would need a STIPULATIO.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Exercises (application)
cards.front: Ex 4: Gaia asks her debtor Hermes to pay Felix a 700 loan; Hermes pays only 500, which Felix accepts. MUTUUM, and Gaia's claim?
cards.back:
Yes — loan by delegation: MUTUUM between Gaia and Felix for 500, enforced by CONDICTIO (ACTIO CERTAE CREDITAE PECUNIAE).
• DATIO only 500 → loan debt 500 (cf Case 1).
• Hermes' payment also discharges 500 of his debt to Gaia.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Exercises (application)
cards.front: Ex 7: Kriton keeps Juno's lemon tree, moves only his own orange trees into the cellar, and the lemon tree freezes. Contract and liability?
cards.back:
DEPOSITUM (gratuitous custody, arising by DATIO); Kriton breached DILIGENTIA QUAM IN SUIS REBUS — so he is liable.
• He treated the deposit worse than his own things.
• Juno: ACTIO DEPOSITI DIRECTA for damages.
• Kriton: ACTIO DEPOSITI CONTRARIA for any expenses of care.

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Exercises (application)
cards.front: Ex 11: Iris lends slave Stichus to Ufens; feeding costs 500, then emergency surgery 10.000. What can Ufens recover?
cards.back:
Not the 500 for food (ordinary upkeep), but the 10.000 necessary medical costs — by the ACTIO COMMODATI CONTRARIA.
• The commodatary carries ordinary costs because he uses the thing.
• Illness costs concern the owner's interest (cf Case 31).

cards.topic: Ch. III — Real contracts: Exercises (application)
cards.front: Ex 12: Carus pledges two oxen to Daphne; (a) one belongs to Eros; (c) Daphne treats a sick ox herself and it dies. Claims?
cards.back:
(a) No right in rem in Eros' ox → Daphne demands a substitute pledge (CONTRARIA); (c) Daphne liable for CULPA (DIRECTA).
• The contract arises by DATIO even without power of disposal.
• Pledgee answers for DOLUS, CULPA and CUSTODIA.
